findings.heading: Install Git
findings.proposition: EN states installing Git is mandatory ("You must first install Git"); FR states it is optional ("Vous pouvez d'abord installer Git").
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader may think installing Git is optional when the English original presents it as a required first step.

findings.heading: Install an interface (optional but recommended)
findings.proposition: EN's note lists four things you can do across interfaces: switch between them per project, use the console punctually for unsupported actions, or perform actions directly online on Github. FR keeps only "switch from one to another" and drops the console-fallback and online-action points.
findings.reader_consequence: French readers do not learn that they can fall back to the console for actions their interface lacks, or perform actions directly on Github.com.

findings.heading: Vocabulary, concepts and basic functions
findings.proposition: EN explains that although interfaces will be shown, it is good to keep the vocabulary/concepts in mind to build a mental model, since they will be needed anyway when using interfaces. FR's sentence stops after "we will show how to use interfaces" and omits this rationale.
findings.reader_consequence: French readers lose the stated reason for learning the vocabulary before moving to interface-based instructions.

findings.heading: Commits (Staged changes)
findings.proposition: EN's example says you worked on model specification in one script, and later on a figure in another script. FR's sentence loses the "figure in another script" clause, leaving only the model-specification part before the parenthetical mentions "la figure" with no antecedent.
findings.reader_consequence: French readers hit a mention of "la figure" in the parenthetical that was never introduced in the sentence, making the example confusing.

findings.heading: Local and remote repositories
findings.proposition: EN labels the online copy the *REMOTE* repository; FR mistranslates this as the *ROMPU* ("broken") repository instead of *DISTANT* (remote).
findings.reader_consequence: French readers encounter a nonsensical/incorrect label ("broken" repository) for what is simply the remote copy, which can confuse the local-vs-remote distinction the section is teaching.

findings.heading: In console (Create a new branch)
findings.proposition: EN's three commands all operate on the same branch name "my-new-branch", illustrating two-step vs one-step (shortcut) ways to reach the identical result. FR's third line silently uses a different branch name ("ma-nouvelle-branche") while the comment still says "Les deux à la fois" (both at once), so the shortcut line no longer refers to the branch created by the first two lines.
findings.reader_consequence: A reader following the FR code block literally creates two different branches ("my-new-branch" and "ma-nouvelle-branche") while the comment claims the third command is just a shortcut equivalent to the first two.

findings.heading: Git + Github workflow (Process overview, step 5)
findings.proposition: EN step 5 says merging the working branch into main is done "to transfer the changes". FR instead says this is done "afin de créer une nouvelle branche" (in order to create a new branch).
findings.reader_consequence: French readers are told that merging into main creates a new branch, which contradicts the actual purpose of this step (transferring changes into main) and duplicates what branch-creation (step 2) already does.

findings.heading: In Github: submitting pull requests
findings.proposition: EN states a PR can be submitted directly from the website or from Github Desktop. FR drops "Desktop", saying only "à partir du site Web ... ou à partir de Github", which duplicates the website option instead of naming the Github Desktop application.
findings.reader_consequence: French readers lose the information that Github Desktop itself supports submitting a pull request, since the sentence now names the website twice.

findings.heading: Pull and push changes up to Github (Note)
findings.proposition: EN's note ends with an actionable recommendation: "so it is better to push when you are done with introducing changes on the task that you were working on." FR's note stops after comparing reverting pushed vs unpushed changes and omits this recommendation.
findings.reader_consequence: French readers get the risk comparison (easier to revert unpushed changes) but lose the practical guidance on when to push.
